COVID-19: 24 hours on the frontline

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
They are risking their lives to fight COVID 19, health workers document 24 hours at the Coalface of the virus

Summary:
The patients will keep coming and they will be fighting for space, for oxygen, for treatment and all the medical staff on the frontline will keep fighting for them, for every sick South African. COVId 19 has washed over the world like a tsunami and the doctors and nurses that are at the coalface will still be treading water for a long time to come. Every day they turn up and put their lives and their families lives at risk. They are exhausted and scared for tomorrow and the day after that, they are worried about when the resources run out, when they have no more to give. But inspire of it all they turn up every day and fight harder. In the CoVID 19 pandemic that the world will never forget these men and woman are the hero’s

These are their stories straight form the field. Raw and uncensored they documented their lives at the coalface of COVID 19 using only their cellphones, because they want South Africa to understand the gravity of this virus.

00:00 – 00:22
While we all focus on trying to stay home, Health care professionals have been working harder than ever before
Every day they wake up, show up and risk their lives to save another.
three doctors.
From three different hospitals in Johannesburg, Gauteng
Used their cellphone camera’s to take us into their world

0:22 – 1:43
Thato video:
Length of shift
Vo: Thato Moloko works in the medical emergency unit at Baragwanath. When she started filming for us Alcohol had JUST been unbanned in South Africa AND THERE WAS A SURGE IN ADMISSIONS
Thato video:
Its going for 1am since handover at 9am constant flow of patients, around 60 at a time. Lost two patients
THATO:
The plan initially was for our unit to be the clean emergency unit but because of the numbers and that the fact that we actually don't have enough staff to separate that we are now just generic and we are treating over positives next to nonprofit patients. Harper. The same cubicle sometimes
So now we are seeing patients coming in positive or we diagnosed and positive because they are waiting so long and you are sitting next to a Grammy that came in because she had a headache.
THATO VIDEO
New way to triage COVID patients

1:43 – 2:05
Dr Tumi Moshoeshoe Is a Medical registrar at Charlotte Makeke Johannesburg Academic hospital she has been working in the COVID ward since their first patient arrived back in March.
When Tumi started recording her life on the frontline she had been working for 21 days straight

2:05 – 3:49
Tumi Video:
Being on call and I’m tired
Thumi: The hardest part about being in the covered Ward is how very quickly patients change condition.
And deteriorate.
Tumi video:
She was just in a resus
Days passes and that patients dies
She is filling in death certificates





3:50 – 4:33
Thato: Before covered earlier on in the year it was busy because Barra is busy anyway busy was maximum 20 patients. But now since covered we are seeing or we've seen a maximum about 60 patients on the floor at one time.
We are seeing too many patients for the amount of recess space that we have.
Thato video:
Slitting one oxygen port into multiple supplies
Patients are receiving less that they should be

4:34 – 6:12
Tom intro
VO: DR. Tom Boyles is an infectious disease consultant currently working as the Clinical lead of intermediate care at NASRAC. He has also worked on the Ebola outbreaks in West Africa.
Tom: A month or so ago it become evident that Gauteng was going to more beds with oxygen and we couldn’t see new beds to created
LINK: At this time the NASREC field hospital had been opened in Johannesburg without any oxygen. So Tom and HIS partner in work and life Lynn Wilkinson put out a plea for oxygen concentrators and within days they had 50 ready to be installed in Nasrec
within about six days we had our first patients admitted onto oxygen concentrators within Nazareth.
TOM: This is an oxygen concentrator. How it works and that they now have 100
VO: Working In partnership with the Gauteng department of health Lynn and Tom are managing the intermediate care section at Nasrec.
TOM VIDEO:
Intros Lynn
Sip of coffee
Physiotherapists -

6:13 – 6:40
the big work comes from the physiotherapy department
Stress and anxiety. Reduce your immune system. Your immune system is the front line against Corbett. And. The more stressed you are. The more Corbett wins.
if you're panicking you breathe very well.
You need breathing exercises to get you through
Tumi video
Her doing exercises with a patient and celebrating how well they are doing

6:41 – 7:28
Soon after the second ban on alcohol Thato sent us this video
ThatoVideo: tonight has been the calmest night in ages
Been a good night
The ban of alcohol has had a positive effect in the total patient in flux for all departments from trauma medical paediatric etc. and also in terms of complications of illness as well we've seen less.
Video thato: we have space to see patients and resus with feeling rushed





7:29 – 8:43
Tumi video
7:10 and Im going to do a weekend shift
HIGHflow patient can’t be helped as the parts are out of stock
Her husband died
So I just had to tell her Look I know you said I know you're in a bad place today but tonight we're fighting for your life. I need you to use this double oxygen so I put I put to put a face mask into the nasal prong so that I could add 60 percent plus 20 percent and hopefully get 80 percent.
Who knows if that worked.
video: Have to do something for our patients
she got an ICU bed. The next day. So it's not to say that the bed will never come.you just have to survive the waiting list


8:44 – 8:54
The Gauteng department of health has subsequently opened a new ICU unit at Charlotte Maxeke with 29 beds, of which they say only 12 have ever been used.

8:55- 9:47
Every day That and Thato and her team show up for work they are faced with life and death decisions
Video: putting oxygen on an elder woman
Mumma we are going to put this mask on your face
Don’t take it off okay it is going to help you breathe
It's the worst feeling to know that what you're doing is not enough. And that's been the reality the past three months. It's gotten. To a point where we choose. Who is with a recess attempt. Or we choose who's with oxygen. Because we don't have enough resources for everyone. And when you have to tell a family member that. Their loved one died and you did everything you could. But technically it's not true.

9:47 – 10:12
TOM: Many people understandably feel the stress but it isn’t just the dr’s and nurses it is also affecting the patients, because people are dying next to them. patients are getting PTSD
Tom Video: glad to get out PPE’s and go and see my children

10:12 – 10:28
LINK: Watching patients get sick or die has taken an emotional toll on Tumi, Thato and Tom but treating and burying their own health care colleagues is a new part of the fight they are having to adjust to. Thato actuallu contracted COVID about three weeks ago

10:30 – 11:02
Thato video:
Glad to be able to take a walk and be out of the house
Walking in her complex – visual
It’s a weird to feeling to know that you are statistic and that you are more human than you would like to admit
not being able to fend for myself but not being able to be home. With my mom. Was tough like having to stay alone because it's more dangerous for me to go home. That was the worst part of it. I think that had a whole mental health situation that went on the loneliness the depression and anxiety that hit me

11:03 – 11:22
After working for 21 days straight Tumi also started to get sick
Tumi video: Tumi getting tested scene
Luckily Out of her team of 24, Tumi is one of 4 dr who haven’t yet contracted covid

11:23 – 11:52
Although tom’s wife Lynn tested Positive, but both him and his children have managed to not get the virus
Video: Family in the kitchen
Right now I take precautions. I changed my clothes before I come home I wash my hands if I have had a couple of episodes of symptoms. When I tested and tested negative but as soon as I have had any symptoms I've remove myself from my children and had a test and so far they've all been negative
unlike many respiratory illnesses children also themselves don't suffer. If if if this had been an illness like many respiratory illnesses that predominately affect children. Then I would have taken my children for a long long long long ago and I wouldn't have wouldn't have
Video: family say good-bye in the morning

11:53 – 12:23
LINK: Because this virus is so contagious most patients die alone, which means as their dr you may be the last person they see.
VO: On Tuesday this week Tumi had to help a patient that had been in her ward for nearly 30 days say good-bye on video call.
Tumi: helping a patient saying good bye to his family
I love you and I miss you

12:23 – 13:00
Thato vide: Nurses and Dr’s sing in the ward
For me personally if it wasn't for the team that I'm in and the kind of camaraderie and
The closeness that we've kind of gotten in the last couple of months I would probably have broken down a lot more because we all have cried. We've all had emotional moments
Thato video: end of a few long shifts in a row. I just want to go home


Promo

Health workers have been hailed as the heroes of the COVID-19 frontline, but they’re also just human beings doing the best they can. Raw and uncensored --- we go inside their world.

Because hospital wards are no-go zones for journalists, we got three doctors to use their own cameras and take us into the frontline fight against COVID-19.

Using their own camera’s three doctors from some of the biggest hospitals in Africa take us into the heart of the battle against the coronavirus pandemic.
